caption: The perimeter of an empty lot occupies an even number of cells.
content: This page considers the number of cells occupied by an empty lot. For example, the empty lot below occupies 15 cells.

Of these, the perimeter of the empty lot @t{forest_open.1.dr} @t{forest_open.2s.r} occupies 12 cells.
In fact, no matter what shape an empty lot has, its perimeter always occupies @b{an even number of cells}.

This can be explained by the same principle as @g{tips/complete_block/road/parity}{the parity of the number of cells a simple road passes through}.
If we treat the boundary of the empty lot as a road like this, its endpoints are different colors, which means the road passes through an even number of cells.
In particular, it is important that @b{an empty lot made only of perimeter tiles always occupies an even number of cells}.

content.caption: Example
content: Assuming your available tiles are @t{forest_road.2s.lr} @t{forest_road.2t.dr} @t{forest_open.1.dr} @t{forest_open.2s.r} and their rotations, let's solve this Area.

To complete the Area, first we need to create a simple road connecting @m{info}.
Since the endpoints @m{info} are the same color, the road passes through an odd number of cells no matter how it is laid out.

However, this Area has 20 cells (an even number), so this road alone cannot fill the entire Area.
To complete the Area, we need @b{a way to fill an odd number of cells}.

However, with the available tiles, we can only create empty lots that occupy an even number of cells, so empty lots cannot be used to fill an odd number of cells. No matter how the tiles are placed, an odd number of cells will always remain.
Therefore, this Area cannot be completed.
